items.caption: Exact supplied discussion screenshot with a knee radiograph and rickets/Blount/achondroplasia discussion. The bank identifies widened physes and metaphyseal cupping at multiple sites as rickets. Contrast with focal medial proximal tibial beaking/depression in Blount disease; both conditions can be bilateral. Achondroplasia features include FGFR3 gain of function, rhizomelia, metaphyseal flaring/chevron distal femora, champagne-glass pelvis and caudally narrowing lumbar interpedicular distances. Do not reproduce the screenshot error attributing type-II collagen Stickler syndrome to COL1A1: COL2A1 is the relevant type-II collagen gene, and other Stickler genes exist. Vitamin D levels are not universally low in all forms of rickets. User asks for repeat comparison; no answer selection or question identifier visible, so do not infer MISS.
items.placement_heading: Rickets vs Physiologic Genu Varum

items.caption: Exact supplied question screenshot with initial and postoperative foot radiographs: hindfoot varus is the classic keyed risk association for fifth-metatarsal refracture. Avoid treating this as a universally established greatest independent predictor. Consider screw adequacy, recovery/loading and bone health. Young male athletes can have vitamin D deficiency; radiographic union does not guarantee zero refracture risk.
items.placement_heading: Jones fracture — nonoperative nonunion risk

items.caption: Exact supplied question screenshot with weight-bearing foot radiographs: chronic rocker-bottom deformity symptomatic despite bracing, normal hindfoot alignment and mild forefoot abduction. The intended correction is a plantar-based, often plantar-medial biplanar closing wedge at the midfoot deformity apex, usually combined with corrective arthrodesis. Question attributes neuropathy to prior chemotherapy; this is presumed rather than proven by the stated exam. Differentiate isolated prominence removal from correction of substantial nonplantigrade collapse.

Exact supplied Figure 12 screenshot, explicitly identified by Lefko as a good figure for the preceding ankle arthroscopy question. Panel A overlays anterior portals, superficial peroneal nerve branches, anterior tibial neurovascular bundle, tendons, and great saphenous vein; panel B shows posterior portals, sural nerve, posterior tibial neurovascular bundle, and Achilles tendon. Main pearl: anterolateral portal risks superficial peroneal dorsal cutaneous branches and dorsal-foot sensation. Anterocentral portal places the deep peroneal nerve and anterior tibial/dorsalis pedis vessels at risk. The trans-Achilles portal is historical and should not be inferred to be routinely recommended. Figure presented in Jami Ilyas, Ankle Arthroscopy, IntechOpen (2013), https://www.intechopen.com/chapters/43187; supplied image unchanged.
items.placement_heading: Superficial Versus Deep Fibular Nerve Anatomy

items.caption: Exact supplied clinical question screenshot: high-energy open tibial fracture identified as Gustilo type III by the question; keyed ceftriaxone monotherapy versus cefazolin alone. Teach gram-positive coverage for I-II and added gram-negative coverage for III in this exam framework; actual regimens follow institutional protocols and contemporary guidance differs.

Exact supplied question screenshot with intraoperative photo: valgus arthritic knee with posterior lateral femoral condylar hypoplasia. Posterior condylar referencing can underestimate needed external rotation and leave the femoral component internally rotated, predisposing to lateral patellar maltracking or instability. Cross-check transepicondylar axis, Whiteside AP line and gap balance; do not claim fine photo details independently visible.

items.caption: Exact supplied question screenshot with AP and lateral TKA radiographs. The bank describes displaced patellar fracture fragments four months after injury, with 4/5 active extension and only a five-degree extensor lag in a low-demand patient. Observation is the keyed answer. Minimal functional deficit does not justify mesh reconstruction solely for displacement. Confirm patellar component fixation and extensor mechanism competence clinically; acute fractures may require extension immobilization. Fine component fixation details cannot be established from these small panels.

items.caption: Exact supplied enlarged lumbar plexus diagram. A is ilioinguinal (L1); B genitofemoral (L1-L2); C lateral femoral cutaneous (L2-L3 posterior divisions); D femoral (L2-L4 posterior divisions); E obturator (L2-L4 anterior divisions). Green depicts posterior divisions of ventral rami, not dorsal primary rami. Anterior THA with isolated anterolateral thigh sensory loss implicates C; femoral neuropathy adds quadriceps weakness and may reduce the patellar reflex. The upper unlettered branch is iliohypogastric. Preserve the enlarged exact image rather than duplicate the same diagram in the question screenshot.
items.placement_heading: ## Direct anterior THA — LFCN protection and lumbar plexus anatomy

items.caption: Exact supplied Fig. 1 screenshot with original caption. Axial section: black asterisk TFL, white asterisk sartorius, yellow oval lateral femoral cutaneous nerve. The dotted approach enters the superficial thigh fascia laterally over the TFL belly, then follows the subfascial plane to the Hueter interval, preserving the nerve in its fascial tunnel. Open fascia over TFL, work beneath the medial flap, then enter the muscle interval. Rudert et al., BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders 17:57 (2016), https://doi.org/10.1186/s12891-016-0908-z; CC BY 4.0; supplied image unchanged.

items.caption: Exact supplied Fig. 2 screenshot with original caption. Anterolateral thigh dissection: TFL M is tensor fasciae latae, RF M rectus femoris, IP M iliopsoas. The white arrow marks the TFL musculocutaneous perforator at the lateral TFL border, arising from the ascending lateral circumflex femoral artery; it does not mark the LFCN. The labeled femoral neurovascular structures and reflected muscles orient the deeper exposure; the femoral nerve and branches are retracted medially. Rudert et al., BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders 17:57 (2016), https://doi.org/10.1186/s12891-016-0908-z; CC BY 4.0; supplied image unchanged.

items.caption: Exact supplied Q49 screenshot, identifier 22Fund-064, with four axial and sagittal MRI panels. Selected synovial sarcoma; keyed proximal tibiofibular ganglion cyst. The bank describes a lobulated fluid-bright lesion near the proximal tibiofibular joint in the anterior compartment, without internal enhancement. Thin wall or septal enhancement can occur in a ganglion; solid or nodular internal enhancement prompts concern for a neoplasm. Do not claim a fine stalk is independently visible in the small supplied panels. No trauma is only a contextual clue, not an exclusion of hematoma.
